analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security payroll taxes to income above $300,000 and cuts taxes on retirees' benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the 2019-2021 Congress ended, leaving the payroll tax cap unchanged.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, Social Security payroll taxes stop applying once a worker's wages pass a yearly cap (about $133,000 in 2019), no matter how much higher the income goes. This bill would keep collecting the tax on wages above $300,000, count some of that high income in the benefit formula, and raise the income level at which retirees' Social Security checks become taxable from $25,000-$32,000 to $100,000. It died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or any cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people who depend on Social Security, because new tax revenue from very high earners would slow the projected drain on the trust fund that pays benefits. Retirees with incomes between roughly $32,000 and $100,000 also gain, since a smaller share of their benefits would be counted as taxable income.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and middle-income retirees

how_it_helps.text: It applies the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income above $300,000, which currently escape the tax entirely once earnings pass the yearly cap ($132,900 in 2019), shifting a share of program funding onto the highest earners.

It raises to $100,000 the income threshold above which Social Security benefits are included in taxable income, replacing the current $25,000 (single) and $32,000 (joint) thresholds, so fewer moderate-income retirees owe income tax on their benefits.
It directs that any revenue the Treasury loses from the new benefits-taxation threshold be appropriated back to the Social Security trust funds, so retirees' tax cut does not drain the program.

analysis.who_pays: People with wages or self-employment income above $300,000, who would owe the 12.4% payroll tax on income above that line, with a small offsetting bump in their own future benefits (a 3% benefit factor on the extra taxed earnings). Federal taxpayers generally, because the bill replaces the revenue the retiree tax cut removes from the trust funds with general Treasury appropriations.

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to earnings under $300,000 and over $300,000, but the stretch between the current cap (~$132,900) and $300,000 stays untaxed, leaving a 'donut hole' that limits how much revenue the bill actually raises and sparing six-figure earners in between.

High earners do get slightly larger benefits under the new 3% benefit factor on income above $300,000, which returns part of the new tax to the people least likely to need it and slightly reduces the revenue available to close the financing gap.

Funding the retiree tax cut through annual general-Treasury appropriations, rather than the trust funds' own dedicated tax, adds a claim on the general budget and depends on Congress appropriating the money each year.
Applying the higher benefits-taxation threshold to all taxable years ending after enactment, with the Treasury transfer layered on top, would add near-term complexity to federal budget accounting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a modest tax on a small group of very high earners in exchange for shoring up the program most retirees depend on, plus a tax cut for middle-income beneficiaries. The main honest objection is design, not purpose: the donut hole between the current cap and $300,000 means the bill raises less money per dollar of burden than simply lifting the cap, and part of the new revenue is spent on the retiree tax cut. It is a genuine solvency measure, but a partially leaky one, and it never moved far enough for the Congressional Budget Office or Social Security actuaries to score how much it actually would have helped.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Crist introduced the bill on January 15, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over payroll taxes.
On March 1, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Worker and Family Support, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor during the entire two-year Congress.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the payroll tax cap, who kept paying no Social Security tax on income above about $133,000, and whose future benefits will continue to face the program's projected financing shortfall. The trust-fund gap this bill would have narrowed was left for a future Congress to close through some combination of higher taxes or lower benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the payroll tax cap

for.name: Rep. Charlie Crist
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Richard Neal)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Social Security payroll taxes
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat first at full committee, then in the Subcommittee on Worker and Family Support, from March 2019 until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member signed on from either party, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors.

industries.note: They would have owed the 12.4% payroll tax on income above $300,000, income that currently escapes Social Security tax entirely. Their interest in keeping the cap intact ran against the program's solvency, which all beneficiaries rely on.

The bill appropriates general revenue back to the trust funds to replace the retiree tax cut, adding a new draw on the general budget. In exchange, moderate-income retirees pay less tax on their benefits.

industries.industry: Social Security beneficiaries as a group
industries.note: New payroll tax revenue from high earners would extend the life of the trust fund that pays retirement and disability checks, and retirees under $100,000 in income would keep more of their benefits after taxes.
